qti-choice-interaction.qti-prompt: A software founder who grew up in a two-bedroom apartment buys a centuries-old country manor, hires an etiquette coach, and now hosts polished garden parties that impress every guest. Her parents were schoolteachers, and no one in her family has ever held a title or noble rank of any kind. Is "aristocratic" the accurate word for her?
qti-choice-interaction.qti-simple-choice: Yes — owning a historic manor and mastering upper-class manners is exactly what makes a person aristocratic.
No — her manor and manners were bought and learned, not conferred by noble birth; she is rich and refined, but not aristocratic.
Yes — anyone rich enough to live like the nobility counts as aristocratic.
No — "aristocratic" can only describe reigning kings and queens, never landowning families.

qti-content-body.p: Right. 'Aristocratic' pins membership to birth into a hereditary noble class — a rank that cannot be bought or trained for. Her taste and property are real, but they were acquired, so 'rich' and 'refined' fit her; 'aristocratic' does not.

'Aristocratic' requires birth into a hereditary noble class. Money can buy a manor and coaching can polish manners, but neither changes a person's ancestry — and the word isn't limited to reigning royals either; it covers any hereditary nobility. Since her family never held noble rank, she is rich and refined but not aristocratic.
